title: How baby talk gives infant brains a boost
overallInstruction: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.
overallInstructionZh: 你应该用大约20分钟完成第14–26题，这些题目基于下面的阅读文章2。

bodyParagraphs.label: A
sentences: The typical way of talking to a baby – high-pitched, exaggerated and repetitious – is a source of fascination for linguists who hope to understand how ‘baby talk’ impacts on learning.
Most babies start developing their hearing while still in the womb, prompting some hopeful parents to play classical music to their pregnant bellies.
Some research even suggests that infants are listening to adult speech as early as 10 weeks before being born, gathering the basic building blocks of their family’s native tongue.

bodyParagraphs.label: B
sentences: Early language exposure seems to have benefits to the brain – for instance, studies suggest that babies raised in bilingual homes are better at learning how to mentally prioritize information.
So how does the sweet if sometimes absurd sound of infant-directed speech influence a baby’s development?
Here are some recent studies that explore the science behind baby talk.

bodyParagraphs.label: C
sentences: Fathers don’t use baby talk as often or in the same ways as mothers – and that’s perfectly OK, according to a new study.

Mark VanDam of Washington State University at Spokane and colleagues equipped parents with recording devices and speech-recognition software to study the way they interacted with their youngsters during a normal day.
‘We found that moms do exactly what you’d expect and what’s been described many times over,’ VanDam explains.
‘But we found that dads aren’t doing the same thing.
Dads didn’t raise their pitch or fundamental frequency when they talked to kids.’
Their role may be rooted in what is called the bridge hypothesis, which dates back to 1975.
It suggests that fathers use less familial language to provide their children with a bridge to the kind of speech they’ll hear in public.
‘The idea is that a kid gets to practice a certain kind of speech with mom and another kind of speech with dad, so the kid then has a wider repertoire of kinds of speech to practice,’ says VanDam.

bodyParagraphs.label: D
sentences: Scientists from the University of Washington and the University of Connecticut collected thousands of 30-second conversations between parents and their babies, fitting 26 children with audio-recording vests that captured language and sound during a typical eight-hour day.
The study found that the more baby talk parents used, the more their youngsters began to babble.
And when researchers saw the same babies at age two, they found that frequent baby talk had dramatically boosted vocabulary, regardless of socioeconomic status.

‘Those children who listened to a lot of baby talk were talking more than the babies that listened to more adult talk or standard speech,’ says Nairán Ramírez-Esparza of the University of Connecticut.
‘We also found that it really matters whether you use baby talk in a one-on-one context,’ she adds.
‘The more parents use baby talk one-on-one, the more babies babble, and the more they babble, the more words they produce later in life.’

bodyParagraphs.label: E
sentences: Another study suggests that parents might want to pair their youngsters up so they can babble more with their own kind.

Researchers from McGill University and Université du Québec à Montréal found that babies seem to like listening to each other rather than to adults – which may be why baby talk is such a universal tool among parents.
They played repeating vowel sounds made by a special synthesizing device that mimicked sounds made by either an adult woman or another baby.
This way, only the impact of the auditory cues was observed.
The team then measured how long each type of sound held the infants’ attention.
They found that the ‘infant’ sounds held babies’ attention nearly 40 percent longer.
The baby noises also induced more reactions in the listening infants, like smiling or lip moving, which approximates sound making.
The team theorizes that this attraction to other infant sounds could help launch the learning process that leads to speech.
‘It may be some property of the sound that is just drawing their attention,’ says study co-author Linda Polka.
‘Or maybe they are really interested in that particular type of sound because they are starting to focus on their own ability to make sounds.
We are speculating here but it might catch their attention because they recognize it as a sound they could possibly make.’

bodyParagraphs.label: F
sentences: In a study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, a total of 57 babies from two slightly different age groups – seven months and eleven and a half months – were played a number of syllables from both their native language (English) and a non-native tongue (Spanish).
The infants were placed in a brain-activation scanner that recorded activity in a brain region known to guide the motor movements that produce speech.
The results suggest that listening to baby talk prompts infant brains to start practicing their language skills.

‘Finding activation in motor areas of the brain when infants are simply listening is significant, because it means the baby brain is engaged in trying to talk back right from the start, and suggests that seven-month-olds’ brains are already trying to figure out how to make the right movements that will produce words,’ says co-author Patricia Kuhl.

Another interesting finding was that while the seven-month-olds responded to all speech sounds regardless of language, the brains of the older infants worked harder at the motor activations of non-native sounds compared to native sounds.
The study may have also uncovered a process by which babies recognize differences between their native language and other tongues.

questions.evidence: the baby brain is engaged in trying to talk back right from the start
questions.reasoning: what babies hear 对应 simply listening；own efforts to create speech 对应 trying to talk back。
questions.distractors: A研究父亲的桥梁作用；B研究婴儿话语量与词汇增长。

questions.stem: the advantage for the baby of having two parents each speaking in a different way
questions.stemZh: 父母双方各用不同方式说话给婴儿带来的好处
questions.evidence: a kid gets to practice a certain kind of speech with mom and another kind of speech with dad, so the kid then has a wider repertoire
questions.reasoning: two parents each speaking differently 对应 mom 与 dad 的两种 speech；优势是 wider repertoire。
questions.distractors: B关注一对一婴儿语和咿呀发声；C关注脑部运动区。

questions.stem: the connection between the amount of baby talk babies hear and how much vocalising they do themselves
questions.stemZh: 婴儿听到的婴儿语数量与其自身发声量之间的联系
questions.evidence: The more parents use baby talk one-on-one, the more babies babble
questions.reasoning: the more ... the more ... 直接建立话语输入量与 babble 发声量的正相关。
questions.distractors: A没有测量发声量；C讨论脑激活而非咿呀发声数量。

questions.stem: Researchers at Washington State University used ________, together with specialised computer programs, to analyse how parents interacted with their babies during a normal day.
questions.stemZh: 华盛顿州立大学研究人员使用________并配合专门计算机程序分析亲子互动。
questions.evidence: colleagues equipped parents with recording devices and speech-recognition software
questions.reasoning: specialised computer programs 对应 speech-recognition software；与之并列使用的是 recording devices。
questions.distractors: software 已由题干 computer programs 改写，不能再填。

questions.stem: The study revealed that ________ tended not to modify their ordinary speech patterns when interacting with their babies.
questions.stemZh: 研究显示，________与婴儿互动时往往不改变日常说话方式。
questions.evidence: Dads didn’t raise their pitch or fundamental frequency when they talked to kids.
questions.reasoning: not modify ordinary speech patterns 对应 didn’t raise pitch or fundamental frequency；主语是 dads/fathers。
questions.distractors: mothers 会按典型婴儿语方式改变说话方式。

questions.stem: According to an idea known as the ________, they may use a more adult type of speech to prepare infants for the language they will hear outside the family home.
questions.stemZh: 根据称为________的观点，他们可能使用更成人化的语言帮助婴儿适应家庭外语言。
questions.evidence: Their role may be rooted in what is called the bridge hypothesis
questions.reasoning: known as 对应 is called，原文两词名称直接填入。
questions.distractors: familial language 是语言类型，不是该观点名称。

questions.stem: Hearing baby talk from one parent and ‘normal’ language from the other expands the baby’s ________ of types of speech which they can practise.
questions.stemZh: 一位家长说婴儿语、另一位说正常语言，会扩展婴儿可练习言语类型的________。
questions.evidence: the kid then has a wider repertoire of kinds of speech to practice
questions.reasoning: expands 对应 wider；空后 of types of speech 与 repertoire of kinds of speech 对齐。
questions.distractors: bridge 是作用机制的比喻，不符合空后的 of types。

questions.stem: Another study ... recorded speech and sound using special ________ that the babies were equipped with.
questions.stemZh: 另一项研究使用婴儿穿戴的特殊________记录语言和声音。
questions.evidence: fitting 26 children with audio-recording vests that captured language and sound
questions.reasoning: equipped with 对应 fitting ... with；记录声音的穿戴物是 vests。
questions.distractors: recording devices 属于前一项父母研究；本研究设备穿在婴儿身上。

questions.stem: Those who had heard a lot of baby talk in infancy had a much larger ________ than those who had not.
questions.stemZh: 婴儿期听到大量婴儿语的孩子拥有大得多的________。
questions.evidence: frequent baby talk had dramatically boosted vocabulary
questions.reasoning: much larger 改写 dramatically boosted；被提升的是 vocabulary。
questions.distractors: babble 是婴儿期发声行为，不是两岁时 larger 所修饰的可数结果。

questions.stem: a reference to a change which occurs in babies’ brain activity before the end of their first year
questions.stemZh: 提到婴儿未满一岁前脑活动发生的变化
questions.evidence: the seven-month-olds responded to all speech sounds regardless of language, the brains of the older infants worked harder at the motor activations of non-native sounds compared to native sounds
questions.reasoning: 比较七个月与十一个半月婴儿的脑部运动激活，显示一岁前发生变化。官方答案为F。
questions.distractors: A谈出生前听觉；E谈婴儿对声音的注意，没有比较年龄导致的脑活动变化。原书指令虽写A–E，答案页仍明确给F。
